data.name: tweak.ai.copilotButton.title

data.name: tweak.ai.copilotButton.why

data.name: tweak.ai.copilotPolicy.why
data.value: Sets Microsoft's "Turn off Windows Copilot" policy for your account.

data.name: tweak.ai.copilotPolicy.warning
data.value: Microsoft says this policy covers the older built-in Copilot panel. On newer versions Copilot is an app: remove the Copilot app as well.

data.name: tweak.ai.copilotApp.warning

data.name: tweak.ai.recallOff.why

data.name: tweak.ai.recallOff.warning
data.value: Only matters on Copilot+ PCs that have Recall. Check afterwards that old snapshots are gone in Settings > Privacy & security > Recall & snapshots.

data.name: tweak.ai.clickToDo.why
data.value: Click to Do analyses what is on your screen to suggest AI actions. This turns it off with Microsoft's policy. Only present on Copilot+ PCs.

data.name: tweak.ai.paint.why

data.name: tweak.ai.notepad.why

data.name: tweak.ai.edgeCopilot.why

data.name: tweak.ai.edgeCopilot.warning

data.value: For a few minutes PC Doctor will load the processor and memory on purpose, and the disk too if the disk test is ticked (it writes a temporary test file and deletes it). m3.lolbin.title
data.value: "{0}" starts a built-in Windows tool in a way malware often does ({1})

data.name: m3.lolbin.why
data.value: The program itself is a normal part of Windows, so a signature check finds nothing wrong. What stands out is what it is told to do at every start: for example run hidden or encoded commands, or download and run something. Some legitimate software does this too, so this is a reason to look, not proof. The exact reasons are listed in the evidence.

data.name: m3.lolbin.action
data.value: If you do not recognise what set this up, disable it (this can be undone) and run a full Microsoft Defender scan from the Protection page.

data.name: m11.rtp.why
data.value: Files are not checked when they are downloaded or opened.

data.name: m11.rtp.action
data.value: Turn it on in Windows Security > Virus & threat protection > Manage settings. PC Doctor never changes Defender settings itself.

data.name: m11.tamper.why
data.value: Without it, malware running as administrator can turn Defender off.

data.name: m11.tamper.action

data.name: m11.signatures.action

data.name: m11.firewall.why

data.name: m11.firewall.action
data.value: Turn the firewall back on in Windows Security > Firewall & network protection, unless another firewall product manages it.

data.name: m11.uac.title
data.value: User Account Control is turned off

data.name: m11.uac.why
data.value: Every program you start runs with full administrator rights.

data.name: m11.uac.action
data.value: Set EnableLUA back to 1 (Control Panel > User Accounts > Change User Account Control settings) and restart.

data.name: m11.uacPrompt.title
data.value: Administrators are elevated without a prompt

data.name: m11.uacPrompt.why
data.value: Programs can gain administrator rights silently.

data.name: m11.uacPrompt.action
data.value: Move the User Account Control slider back to the default level.

data.name: m11.secureBoot.why
data.value: Malware that loads before Windows (bootkits) is not blocked.

data.name: m11.secureBoot.action
data.value: Turn Secure Boot on in the UEFI/BIOS settings. Check the PC maker's instructions first.

data.name: m11.secureBoot.legacy
data.value: No UEFI Secure Boot state: the PC may be booting in legacy BIOS mode.

data.name: m11.tpm.title
data.value: The TPM is missing, disabled or not activated

data.name: m11.tpm.why
data.value: BitLocker, Windows Hello and Windows 11 rely on the TPM.

data.name: m11.tpm.action
data.value: Enable the TPM (often called PTT or fTPM) in the UEFI/BIOS settings.

data.name: m11.bitlocker.title
data.value: The system drive is not encrypted

data.name: m11.bitlocker.why
data.value: If the PC is lost or stolen, its files can be read by removing the drive.

data.name: m11.bitlocker.action
data.value: Turn on BitLocker or Device Encryption in Settings, and store the recovery key somewhere safe.

data.name: m11.hvci.why
data.value: Memory integrity stops malicious or vulnerable drivers from running kernel code. Some older drivers are incompatible, and it can cost some gaming performance.

data.name: m11.hvci.action
data.value: Windows Security > Device security > Core isolation lists the drivers that block it.

data.name: m11.lsa.why
data.value: Credential-stealing tools can read sign-in secrets from the LSA process more easily.

data.name: m11.lsa.action
data.value: Turn on Local Security Authority protection in Windows Security > Device security > Core isolation.

data.name: m11.smb1.title

data.name: m11.smb1.why

data.name: m11.smb1.action
data.value: Remove "SMB 1.0/CIFS File Sharing Support" in Windows Features, unless an old device you use needs it.

data.name: m11.rdp.action

data.name: m5.noPagefile.action

data.name: m5.dumpFailed.why
data.value: The crash happened, but the file that would explain it was not written (volmgr event 161).

data.name: m5.dumpFailed.action
data.value: Check that the page file is system-managed and the system drive has free space.

data.name: m5.bsod.action.unknown

data.name: m5.forcedOff.title
data.value: The PC was forced off while unresponsive ({0} times)

data.name: m5.forcedOff.why
data.value: Windows recorded that the power button was held down. That usually means the PC froze.

data.name: m5.forcedOff.action
data.value: Note what was running when it froze. Check graphics and storage drivers and temperatures.

data.name: m5.forcedOff.action.related
data.value: {0} related events (graphics or storage resets, hardware errors) happened just before. See the evidence.

data.name: m5.powerLoss.title
data.value: The PC stopped without shutting down ({0} times)

data.name: m5.powerLoss.why
data.value: There was no blue screen and no power-button press: power was lost or the PC hung hard.

data.name: m5.powerLoss.action
data.value: Check hardware errors below, the power supply and cabling, temperatures, and remove overclocks.

data.name: m5.powerLoss.action.related
data.value: {0} related events (graphics or storage resets, hardware errors) happened just before. See the evidence.

data.name: m5.wheaFatal.why
data.value: The processor or memory reported an error it could not correct (WHEA-Logger 18).

data.name: m5.wheaPcie.title
data.value: {0} corrected PCI Express errors from device {1}

data.name: m5.wheaPcie.why
data.value: Corrected errors are fixed by the hardware, but many of them can point to a loose card, a riser cable or link power saving problems.

data.name: m5.wheaPcie.action
data.value: Reseat the device, update chipset drivers and BIOS. The vendor and device IDs identify the device.

data.name: m5.wheaCorrected.why
data.value: The hardware fixed these itself, but they often precede uncorrectable errors on unstable overclocks or failing memory.

data.name: m5.tdr.title
data.value: The display driver stopped responding and recovered {0} times

data.name: m5.tdr.why
data.value: Windows reset the graphics driver (Display event 4101). Repeated resets can end in a freeze or blue screen.

data.name: m5.tdr.action
data.value: Install the current driver from the GPU maker, remove GPU overclocks and check GPU temperatures. Do not edit the TDR registry keys.

data.name: m5.firmwareLimit.title
data.value: Firmware limited the processor speed ({0} times)

data.name: m5.firmwareLimit.why
data.value: This is not a failure. It means the CPU was slowed, often because of heat or power limits (Kernel-Processor-Power 37).

data.name: m5.firmwareLimit.action
data.value: If the PC feels slow, check cooling and the power plan. On laptops this is common on battery.

data.name: m5.storage.disk7.title
data.value: The disk reported bad blocks ({0} events)

data.name: m5.storage.disk7.why
data.value: Part of the disk could not be read reliably. Data in those blocks may be lost.

data.name: m5.storage.disk11.title
data.value: The disk controller reported errors ({0} events)

data.name: m5.storage.disk11.why
data.value: Commands to the disk failed. Cables, ports, the controller driver or the disk itself can cause this.

data.name: m5.storage.disk51.title
data.value: Errors while paging to disk ({0} events)

data.name: m5.storage.disk51.why
data.value: Windows had trouble writing memory pages to disk, which can cause freezes and crashes.

data.name: m5.storage.ntfs55.why
data.value: NTFS found damaged file system structures. Files on that volume may be affected.

data.name: m5.storage.ntfs98.title
data.value: A volume needs a file system check ({0} events)

data.name: m5.storage.ntfs98.why
data.value: NTFS marked a volume as needing repair.

data.name: m5.storage.ntfs50.why
data.value: Data Windows had cached could not be written to disk, so some changes may be lost.

data.name: m5.storage.ntfs140.why
data.value: Often logged when a USB drive is removed without ejecting. Repeated on an internal disk, it can point to a storage problem.

data.name: m5.storage.storport129.title
data.value: The storage driver reset the disk ({0} events)

data.name: m5.storage.storport129.why
data.value: The disk stopped answering and was reset. This often comes before freezes.

data.name: m5.storage.storport153.why
data.value: Reads or writes timed out and were retried. Firmware, drivers, cables or a failing disk can cause this.

data.name: m5.storage.disk157.title
data.value: A disk was removed unexpectedly ({0} events)

data.name: m5.storage.disk157.why
data.value: Normal for USB drives pulled out without ejecting. For an internal disk it can mean a loose connection.

data.name: m5.storage.action
data.value: Check the disk health section, update storage drivers and SSD firmware, and check cables.

data.name: m5.storage.action.backup
data.value: Back up your files now, then check the disk health section and run a read-only disk check (chkdsk /scan).

data.name: m5.serviceCrash.why
data.value: A background service crashed. Windows may have restarted it, but whatever it provides was interrupted.

data.name: m5.serviceCrash.action
data.value: Update or reinstall the app the service belongs to.

data.name: m5.serviceStart.title
data.value: {0} services failed to start or timed out

data.name: m5.serviceStart.why
data.value: This is common on healthy PCs (for example, a service for a device that is not present). It matters only if something you use does not work.

data.name: m5.serviceStart.action
data.value: If a feature you use is broken, update or reinstall the app that owns the service named in the evidence.

data.name: m5.app.title
data.value: {0} crashed {1} times and stopped responding {2} times

data.name: m5.app.why
data.value: Repeated crashes of one app usually come from that app or a plug-in it loads, not from Windows.

data.name: m5.app.action
data.value: Update or reinstall the app. If the faulting module in the evidence belongs to another product, update that product.

data.name: m7.check.disks.none
data.value: Windows' storage management data could not be read.

data.name: m7.check.usbRaid.detail
data.value: Windows does not pass health data through most USB enclosures and RAID controllers. If smartctl is installed it can read them; PC Doctor does not ship it.

data.name: m7.health.healthy
data.value: Windows reports Healthy. This is the drive's own self-assessment, not a guarantee.

data.name: m7.unhealthy.title
data.value: Back up now: {0} reports it is failing

data.name: m7.unhealthy.why
data.value: The drive's own monitoring says it is degrading. Drives in this state can stop working without further warning.

data.name: m7.backupNow
data.value: Back up your files now. Then replace the drive or contact the PC maker.

data.name: m7.uncorrected.why
data.value: Uncorrected errors mean data could not be read or written correctly.

data.name: m7.latency.title
data.value: {0} took more than {1} seconds to answer at least once

data.name: m7.latency.why
data.value: Very slow responses cause freezes and can be an early sign of a failing drive or connection.

data.name: m7.latency.action
data.value: Update SSD firmware and storage drivers, check cables, and keep a current backup.

data.name: m7.wear.title
data.value: {0} has used {1}% of its rated endurance

data.name: m7.wear.why
data.value: SSDs wear with writes. Once the counter passes its rated maximum the drive is outside its rated life, though many keep working.

data.name: m7.wear.action
data.value: Keep backups current and plan a replacement.

data.name: m7.nvme.badLog
data.value: The drive returned a health log PC Doctor could not read.

data.name: m7.nvmeCritical.title
data.value: Back up now: {0} raised a critical warning ({1})

data.name: m7.nvmeCritical.why
data.value: The NVMe drive itself flagged a critical condition (spare space, temperature, reliability or read-only mode).

data.name: m7.nvmeMedia.title
data.value: {0} logged {1} media and data integrity errors

data.name: m7.nvmeMedia.why
data.value: The drive could not recover some data it stored. If this number grows, the drive is failing.

data.name: m7.nvmeTemp.why
data.value: Hot NVMe drives slow themselves down and wear faster.

data.name: m7.nvmeTemp.action
data.value: Improve airflow or add a heatsink to the drive.

data.name: m7.smart.title
data.value: Disk {0} reports reallocated or unreadable sectors

data.name: m7.smart.why
data.value: SMART attributes 5, 187, 197 and 198 count sectors the drive had to replace or could not read. Rising counts predict failure.

data.value: Devices with problems in Device Manager

data.name: m9.check.devices.detail
data.value: {0} devices with problems; {1} not connected or disabled by you (hidden).

data.name: m9.device.action
data.value: Open Device Manager, check the device's status, and install the driver from the device or PC maker.

data.name: m9.code.1
data.value: The device is not configured correctly (code 1).

data.name: m9.code.3
data.value: The driver may be damaged, or Windows is low on memory (code 3).

data.name: m9.code.12
data.value: The device cannot find enough free resources (code 12).

data.name: m9.code.14
data.value: The device needs a restart to work (code 14).

data.name: m9.code.18
data.value: The driver needs to be reinstalled (code 18).

data.name: m9.code.19
data.value: Windows cannot start the device because its registry configuration is damaged (code 19).

data.name: m9.code.24
data.value: The device is not present, not working, or missing drivers (code 24).

data.name: m9.code.39
data.value: The driver is corrupted or missing (code 39).

data.name: m9.code.43
data.value: Windows stopped the device because it reported problems (code 43).

data.name: m9.code.48
data.value: The driver was blocked because it has known problems (code 48).

data.name: m9.code.52
data.value: Windows cannot verify the driver's signature (code 52).

data.name: m9.unsigned.why
data.value: Windows normally requires signed drivers. Unsigned ones were installed with signing checks relaxed, and their origin cannot be verified.

data.name: m9.unsigned.action
data.value: Replace them with signed drivers from the device maker, or remove the device software if you do not use it.

data.name: m9.old.title
data.value: {0} third-party drivers are more than {1} years old

data.name: m9.old.why
data.value: Old drivers are not necessarily a problem. They are worth updating only if the device misbehaves or appears in crashes.

data.name: m9.old.action
data.value: If one of these devices causes trouble, check Windows Update and the device maker for a newer driver.

data.name: m9.winring0.title
data.value: Vulnerable WinRing0 driver installed by software in {0}

data.name: m9.winring0.why
data.value: WinRing0 (CVE-2020-14979) lets any program on the PC read and write hardware directly. Defender flags it as HackTool:Win32/Winring0.

data.name: m9.winring0.action
data.value: Update the monitoring or fan-control app in that folder to a version that no longer uses WinRing0, or uninstall it.

data.value: Third-party drivers named in crash dumps

data.name: m10.check.noDesign
data.value: The battery does not report its design capacity.

data.name: m10.check.detail
data.value: Holds {0} of {1} mWh as designed ({2}%); {3} charge cycles.

data.name: m10.worn.title
data.value: The battery holds {0}% of its original charge

data.name: m10.replace.title
data.value: The battery holds only {0}% of its original charge

data.name: m10.worn.why
data.value: Batteries lose capacity with age and charge cycles. The 80% and 60% thresholds are PC Doctor's rule of thumb, not a manufacturer limit.

data.name: m10.worn.action
data.value: Expect shorter battery life. No action is needed unless it no longer lasts long enough for you.

data.name: m10.replace.action
data.value: Consider replacing the battery through the PC maker or an authorized service.

data.name: page.crashes.subtitle
data.value: Blue screens, freezes and sudden power-offs from the last 30 days, with the driver Microsoft's debugger names when the dump files can be read.

data.name: crashes.empty
data.value: No crashes, freezes or hardware errors were recorded in the period checked.

data.name: crashes.deep.body
data.value: Dump files name the driver that crashed, but Windows only lets administrators read them. A Deep Scan reads them through PC Doctor's helper.

data.name: m5.check.dumpAnalysis.debugger
data.value: Windows debugger analysed {0} of {1} dump files.

data.name: m5.check.dumpAnalysis.offline
data.value: The Windows debugger is not installed. The stop code was read from {0} of {1} dump files without it.

data.name: m5.culprit.title
data.value: {0} of {1} blue screens in {2} days name {3} ({4}), stop codes {5}

data.name: m5.culprit.why.unknown
data.value: Microsoft's debugger found this driver on the crashing code path. PC Doctor does not know which product it belongs to; its file properties name the maker.

data.name: m5.culprit.action.unknown
data.value: Find which program or device installed {0} (its file properties show the maker), then update or remove it.

data.name: m5.culprit.core.title
data.value: {0} of {1} blue screens in {2} days stop inside Windows itself ({3})

data.name: m5.culprit.core.why
data.value: When the debugger can only name the Windows kernel, the real cause is usually elsewhere: a driver that corrupted memory earlier, unstable RAM, or an overclock.

data.name: m5.culprit.core.action
data.value: Remove overclocks, run the Windows Memory Diagnostic, and update recently changed drivers.

data.name: m5.needDebugger.title
data.value: Install the Windows debugger to name the driver behind these blue screens

data.name: m5.needDebugger.why
data.value: Without it PC Doctor can read the stop code from each dump but cannot tell which driver crashed. The module names listed are only what the dump contains, not a verdict.

data.name: m5.needDebugger.action
data.value: Install "Debugging Tools for Windows" from the Windows SDK installer (only that feature is needed), then run a Deep Scan again.

data.name: m5.liveKernelGpu.title
data.value: The graphics hardware hung and was reset {0} times (live kernel reports)

data.name: m5.timeline.dumpFailed
data.value: Crash dump could not be saved

data.name: settings.symbols
data.value: Let the Windows debugger download Microsoft's public symbols

data.name: settings.symbols.note
data.value: Makes crash analysis more precise. Only file names of Windows components are requested from msdl.microsoft.com, over HTTPS. Off by default.

data.name: page.protection.subtitle
data.value: PC Doctor has no antivirus engine of its own. It runs Microsoft Defender and, if you ask, Microsoft's Safety Scanner, and reports exactly what they found.

data.name: page.startup.subtitle
data.value: Everything that starts with Windows, a sign-in, a schedule or an event. Signatures are checked the way Windows checks them, including catalog signatures. Entries are disabled, never deleted.

data.name: page.files.subtitle
data.value: Some files can never be read by any program: locked system files, protected folders, files that live only in the cloud. Instead of claiming to scan everything, PC Doctor lists every file as counted or skipped, with the reason.

data.name: m2.engine.thirdParty
data.value: Your active antivirus is {0}. A Defender scan is not available. Use {0} to scan.

data.name: m2.engine.none
data.value: No active antivirus engine was found, so PC Doctor cannot run a malware scan.

data.name: m2.check.history
data.value: Defender detections in the last 30 days

data.name: m2.detection.active.title
data.value: Defender detected {0} and it is not resolved

data.name: m2.detection.active.why
data.value: Defender's own record says this threat was found and the action against it did not complete.

data.name: m2.detection.active.action
data.value: Open Windows Security > Virus & threat protection > Protection history and choose an action, then run a full scan.

data.name: m2.detection.handled.why
data.value: Defender quarantined or removed it. It is listed so you know it happened.

data.name: m2.detection.handled.action
data.value: No action needed unless you believe it was a false positive; then check the quarantine on the Protection page.

data.name: m2.pua.audit
data.value: Audit only: detected but not blocked.

data.name: m2.pua.title
data.value: Defender does not block potentially unwanted apps

data.name: m2.pua.why
data.value: Bundled adware, browser hijackers and fake "PC optimizers" are often not malware, so Defender lets them in unless PUA blocking is on.

data.name: m2.pua.action
data.value: Turn PUA blocking on. PC Doctor can do it for you, with undo.

data.name: m2.pua.undo
data.value: The policy value is recorded in the change journal and can be removed from the Changes tab.

data.name: m2.scan.onDemand
data.value: Not part of the Health Check: start a Defender scan from the Protection page.

data.name: fix.pua.explain
data.value: Sets the documented Group Policy value that turns on Defender's PUA blocking.

data.name: protection.scan.body
data.value: Defender updates its signatures first. A quick scan takes minutes; a full scan can take hours and the PC stays usable. Defender quarantines what it finds, as it normally does; nothing is deleted.

data.name: protection.result.none
data.value: Defender detected no threats in this scan

data.name: protection.result.handled
data.value: Defender found {0} threats and handled them

data.name: protection.result.remaining
data.value: Defender found {0} threats that still need action

data.name: protection.result.failed
data.value: The scan did not complete, so there is no result

data.name: protection.result.signaturesFailed
data.value: The signature update failed, so this scan used the signatures already on the PC.

data.name: protection.msert.body
data.value: Downloads Microsoft's standalone scanner (about 200 MB, it expires after about 10 days so a fresh copy is always used), checks its signature and runs a quick scan.

data.name: protection.msert.consent
data.value: PC Doctor will download the Microsoft Safety Scanner from microsoft.com, run it only if it is validly signed by Microsoft, and delete it afterwards. It may remove what it detects.

data.name: protection.msert.found
data.value: The Safety Scanner reported {0} infected files

data.name: protection.msert.none
data.value: The Safety Scanner reported no infected files

data.name: protection.restore.consent
m3.check.vt.off
data.value: Off. Turn it on in Settings with your own VirusTotal key to check unsigned binaries by hash.

data.name: m3.unread.error
data.value: Could not be read on this PC.

data.name: m3.action.disable
data.value: Disable it from the Startup page if you do not recognise it. PC Doctor moves it aside instead of deleting it, so it can be put back.

data.name: m3.undo.disable
data.value: Disabling is journaled: the entry can be put back from the Changes tab.

data.name: m3.amsi.title
data.value: The antivirus flagged the startup entry "{0}" as malware

data.name: m3.amsi.why
data.value: PC Doctor passed its script or command line to the installed antivirus through AMSI, and the antivirus called it malicious.

data.name: m3.amsi.action
data.value: Run a full Defender scan from the Protection page.

data.name: m3.vt.why
data.value: This is a second opinion from other vendors' engines, looked up by file hash only. One or two engines alone are often false positives.

data.name: m3.vt.action
data.value: Check where the file came from, and run a Defender scan of its folder.

data.name: m3.accessibility.title
data.value: A sign-in screen tool ({0}) has been replaced or redirected

data.name: m3.accessibility.why
data.value: Replacing Sticky Keys or Ease of Access with another program is a classic way to get an administrator command prompt without a password.

data.name: m3.accessibility.action
data.value: Run DISM and SFC (Repairs page) to restore the original file, and remove the Image File Execution Options debugger value.

data.name: m3.ifeo.title
data.value: "{0}" is set to launch another program instead ({1})

data.name: m3.ifeo.why
data.value: An Image File Execution Options debugger runs whenever the named program starts. Developers use it; so does malware.

data.name: m3.ifeo.action
data.value: If you did not set this up, remove the Debugger value (Registry Editor) and scan with Defender.

data.name: m3.wmi.why
data.value: WMI subscriptions run commands on system events without any file in a startup folder. Few legitimate programs use them.

data.name: m3.wmi.action
data.value: If no management software you use explains it, scan with Defender and remove the subscription.

data.name: m3.appinit.title
data.value: A DLL ({1}) is loaded into every program

data.name: m3.appinit.why
data.value: AppInit_DLLs injects a DLL into every process that loads user32.dll. Microsoft discourages it; malware still uses it.

data.name: m3.appinit.action
data.value: Find which program installed it. If none, scan with Defender.

data.name: m3.winlogon.title
data.value: The Windows sign-in starts something unusual ({0})

data.name: m3.winlogon.why
data.value: Winlogon's Shell and Userinit values are normally explorer.exe and userinit.exe. Anything else runs at every sign-in.

data.name: m3.winlogon.action
data.value: Unless a kiosk or company tool set this, restore the default values and scan with Defender.

data.name: m3.bootexecute.title
data.value: A program runs before Windows starts ({1})

data.name: m3.bootexecute.why
data.value: BootExecute normally only runs autochk. Disk and defragmentation tools sometimes add entries here.

data.name: m3.bootexecute.action
data.value: If you do not recognise it, remove it so the value is "autocheck autochk *".

data.name: m3.lsa.title
data.value: An unknown package is loaded by the Windows security system ({1})

data.name: m3.lsa.why
data.value: LSA packages see passwords at sign-in. A non-Microsoft package here can capture them.

data.name: m3.lsa.action
data.value: Unless security software you installed explains it, scan with Defender and remove the entry.

data.name: m3.forcedExtension.title
data.value: A browser extension is installed by policy: {0}

data.name: m3.forcedExtension.why
data.value: Extensions installed by policy cannot be removed in the browser. Companies do this; so does adware.

data.name: m3.forcedExtension.action
data.value: If this PC is not managed by an organisation, remove the policy value and the extension.

data.name: m3.comhijack.title
data.value: A per-user COM override points to {1}

data.name: m3.comhijack.why
data.value: Registering a COM class per user overrides the system one without administrator rights, a known way to run code in other programs.

data.name: m3.comhijack.action
data.value: Check which program it belongs to; if none, scan with Defender and remove the per-user key.

data.name: m3.unquoted.title
data.value: Service "{0}" has an unquoted path with spaces

data.name: m3.unquoted.why
data.value: Windows may try C:\Program.exe before the real file. If any of those folders is writable, someone can plant a program there.

data.name: m3.unquoted.action
data.value: Update the software that installed the service; its maker should quote the path.

data.name: m3.writable.title
data.value: "{0}" runs with high rights from a file any user can change ({1})

data.name: m3.writable.why
data.value: Replacing that file gives a standard user code that runs as SYSTEM or administrator.

data.name: m3.writable.action
data.value: Reinstall or update the program so it lives in Program Files, or ask its maker to fix the folder permissions.

data.name: m3.badsig.title
data.value: "{0}" has a broken or untrusted signature ({2})

data.name: m3.badsig.why
data.value: The file claims a publisher but the signature does not check out: it was altered, expired, revoked or signed by an untrusted certificate.

data.name: m3.badsig.action
data.value: Reinstall it from its maker, or disable it if you do not recognise it.

data.name: m3.unsigned.title
data.value: "{0}" starts automatically and is not signed ({1})

data.name: m3.unsigned.why
data.value: Unsigned is not malicious: many small tools are unsigned. It only means nobody vouches for the file, so it is worth recognising.

data.name: m3.unsigned.action
data.value: If you recognise it, leave it. If not, look up the file name and consider disabling it.

data.name: m3.missing.title
data.value: "{0}" points to a file that no longer exists

data.name: m3.missing.why
data.value: Usually left behind by an uninstalled program. It does nothing but can cause error messages or delays at startup.

data.name: startup.loading
data.value: Reading startup locations and checking signatures…

data.name: startup.counts
data.value: {0} entries, {1} signed by Microsoft. {2} locations could not be read without administrator rights.

data.name: startup.disable.consent
data.value: "{0}" will stop starting automatically. Nothing is deleted.

data.name: m4.hostsSensitive.title
data.value: The hosts file redirects {0} security, update or banking addresses

data.name: m4.hostsSensitive.why
data.value: Malware edits hosts to stop Windows Update and antivirus updates, or to send you to fake sites.

data.name: m4.hostsSensitive.action
data.value: Remove those lines unless you added them yourself (for example an ad blocker), then scan with Defender.

data.name: m4.hostsCustom.title
data.value: The hosts file has {0} custom redirections

data.name: m4.hostsCustom.why
data.value: Developers and some tools add entries on purpose. Listed so you can check them.

data.name: m4.hostsCustom.action
data.value: Remove any line you do not recognise.

data.name: m4.hostsPath.title
data.value: Windows reads its hosts file from a non-standard folder

data.name: m4.hostsPath.why
data.value: Changing DataBasePath hides a malicious hosts file from anyone who checks the usual one.

data.name: m4.hostsPath.action
data.value: Set DataBasePath back to %SystemRoot%\System32\drivers\etc and scan with Defender.

data.name: m4.proxy.set
data.value: A proxy or auto-configuration script is set.

data.name: m4.proxySet.title
data.value: Web traffic goes through a proxy

data.name: m4.proxySet.why
data.value: Companies, VPNs and some security tools set proxies. Adware sets them too, to inject ads or read traffic.

data.name: m4.proxySet.action
data.value: If you do not use a VPN or company network, turn the proxy off in Settings > Network & internet > Proxy.

data.name: m4.dns.detail
data.value: {0} adapters have DNS servers set by hand.

data.name: m4.dns.title
data.value: Unrecognised DNS servers are set by hand: {0}

data.name: m4.dns.why
data.value: Whoever runs your DNS server decides where every web address leads. Malware sets its own to redirect you.

data.name: m4.dns.action
data.value: If you did not choose these servers, set the adapter back to automatic (DHCP).

data.name: m4.roots.detail
data.value: {0} roots; {1} self-signed roots added recently or by the user.

data.name: m4.root.title
data.value: A root certificate was added recently: {0}

data.name: m4.root.why
data.value: A trusted root lets its owner impersonate any website to this PC. Antivirus, company and developer tools add them legitimately.

data.name: m4.root.action
data.value: If you do not recognise the name, remove it in certmgr.msc (Trusted Root Certification Authorities).

data.name: files.run.body
data.value: Lists every folder without opening any file, so files that live only in OneDrive are not downloaded. Running with administrator rights also lists protected folders.

data.name: files.runElevated.tip
data.value: Uses the backup privilege to list folders protected by permissions. Nothing is read or changed.

data.name: files.stat.folders
data.value: Folders that could not be listed

data.value: {0} files inventoried, {1} skipped (access denied {2}, locked {3}, cloud-only {4}, path errors {5}, links {6}). {7} folders could not be listed, so their files are not counted. {8} hard links were counted once.

data.name: settings.vt
data.value: Check unsigned startup programs on VirusTotal (hash only)

data.name: settings.vt.note
data.value: Needs your own free VirusTotal key. Only SHA-256 hashes are sent, never files. Limited to 4 lookups a minute and 500 a day.

data.name: settings.vt.consent
data.value: When on, PC Doctor sends the SHA-256 hash of unsigned startup programs to virustotal.com with your key. Hashes identify files but do not contain them. VirusTotal's free API is for personal use only.

data.name: page.repairs.subtitle
data.value: Microsoft's own repair tools, run one at a time with their results explained. Anything that needs a restart asks first and says how to recover.

data.name: m6.check.dirty
data.value: System drive needs a disk check

data.name: m6.dirty.no
data.value: The file system is not marked as needing repair.

data.name: m6.dirty.yes
data.value: Windows has marked the file system as needing repair.

data.name: m6.dirtyFinding.title
data.value: Windows will check the system drive at the next restart

data.name: m6.dirtyFinding.why
data.value: The volume is marked dirty: Windows saw a file system problem or an unclean shutdown and will run autochk before it starts.

data.name: m6.dirtyFinding.action
data.value: Back up important files, then restart and let the check finish. It can take a while on large drives.

data.name: m6.memory.never
data.value: No Memory Diagnostic results on this PC.

data.name: m6.memoryErrors.title
data.value: The Windows Memory Diagnostic found errors in the RAM

data.name: m6.memoryErrors.why
data.value: Faulty or unstable memory causes random crashes and can corrupt files as they are saved.

data.name: m6.memoryErrors.action
data.value: Reset memory overclocks (XMP/EXPO) and test again. If errors remain, test one module at a time and replace the faulty one.

data.name: m6.repairs.onDemand
data.value: Not part of the scan: run them from the Repairs page.

data.name: repairs.recommended.body
data.value: Runs DISM to check the component store, asks before repairing it from Windows Update, then runs SFC to repair system files from it. Takes 10 to 40 minutes; the PC stays usable.

data.name: repairs.dism.body
data.value: The store Windows repairs itself from. Check is instant, scan takes minutes, repair downloads fresh copies from Windows Update.

data.name: repairs.dism.Repairable
data.value: The component store is damaged and can be repaired.

data.name: repairs.dism.NonRepairable
data.value: The component store is damaged and DISM cannot repair it. A Windows repair install (in-place upgrade) keeps your files and apps.

data.name: repairs.restore.consent
data.value: DISM will download replacement files from Windows Update and repair the component store. It does not touch your files or apps and cannot be undone, but it only replaces damaged Windows files with Microsoft's originals.

data.name: repairs.sfc.body
data.value: Checks every protected Windows file against the component store and replaces damaged ones.

data.name: repairs.sfc.none
data.value: SFC found no damaged system files.

data.name: repairs.sfc.unrepairable
data.value: SFC could not repair {0} files: {1}. Run the DISM repair first, then SFC again.

data.name: repairs.sfc.noLog
data.value: SFC finished (exit code {0}) but its log could not be read, so the result is unknown.

data.name: repairs.chkdsk.body
data.value: The online check reads the file system without taking the drive offline. A full repair runs before Windows starts.

data.name: repairs.chkdsk.none
data.value: No file system problems found on {0}.

data.name: repairs.chkdsk.fixed
data.value: Problems on {0} were found and fixed.

data.name: repairs.chkdsk.cleanup
data.value: Housekeeping was done on {0}; no errors needed fixing.

data.name: repairs.chkdsk.errors
data.value: Problems were found on {0} that need a repair at restart.

data.name: repairs.chkdsk.unknown
data.value: chkdsk finished on {0} with an unknown result.

data.name: repairs.chkdskFix.title
data.value: Repair the system drive at restart

data.name: repairs.chkdskFix.consent
data.value: Windows will check and repair the system drive before it starts next time. That can take from minutes to hours and must not be interrupted. Back up important files first. This cannot be undone once it runs.

data.name: repairs.reboot.body
data.value: Memory Diagnostic tests the RAM before Windows starts. Defender Offline scans for malware that hides while Windows runs.

data.name: repairs.memory.consent
data.value: Windows will offer to restart now or at the next start. The test takes 10 to 20 minutes; the result appears in the next Health Check.

data.name: repairs.offline.consent
data.value: The PC restarts within a minute into a scan outside Windows (about 15 minutes), then starts Windows again. Save your work first. If BitLocker is on, keep your recovery key at hand in case it is asked for.

data.name: repairs.verifier.body
data.value: Makes Windows stress the named drivers so a faulty one crashes with a clear stop code (0xC4) instead of corrupting memory silently. Only for drivers crash analysis already suspects.

data.name: repairs.verifier.invalid
data.value: Name one to eight third-party driver files such as nvlddmkm.sys, separated by spaces. Windows' own core drivers are not allowed.

data.name: repairs.verifier.consent
data.value: Driver Verifier will check {0} after a restart. The PC may then crash on purpose when a driver misbehaves; that dump names it. If Windows cannot start normally, Verifier turns itself off at the next boot. If it does not, start in Safe Mode and run: verifier /reset

data.name: repairs.restart.body
data.value: The change takes effect after a restart. Save your work. Restart in 30 seconds?

data.name: page.performance.subtitle
data.value: Measure before and after a change. PC Doctor only says "improved" when the difference is both statistically clear and big enough to matter; most tweaks land within measurement noise, and it says so.

data.name: bench.measure.body
data.value: Close other apps and keep the PC plugged in. Each test is repeated until results are stable (at most 10 runs), after two discarded warm-up runs.

data.name: bench.status.game
data.value: Frame capture {0} of 4 in {1}: play the same scene for 60 seconds.

data.name: bench.warn.battery
data.value: Running on battery: results will not be comparable with a plugged-in run.

data.name: bench.warn.justBooted
data.value: Windows started less than 5 minutes ago and is still busy with startup work.

data.name: bench.warn.busy
data.value: The processor is not idle (more than 5% in use). Close other apps first.

data.name: bench.warn.reboot
data.value: A restart is pending. Restart first so both measurements use the same state.

data.name: bench.warn.noDiskspd
